title: Unit 1 Review: Think Like the Exam
description: An exam-technique review of Unit 1: the unit thesis, the three reasoning processes, the SAQ format, and DBQ/LEQ habits that earn the points students most often lose.
essential_question: How do you turn Unit 1 knowledge into exam points?
learning_objectives: State the Unit 1 thesis and attach each major topic to it as evidence.
Apply the three reasoning processes, comparison, causation, and continuity and change, to Unit 1 material.
Describe how to answer each SAQ type and which DBQ/LEQ habits earn the most-lost points.

key_terms.definition: Short-Answer Question: three required questions (Q1 secondary source, Q2 primary source, choice of Q3/Q4 with no stimulus), each scored 0-3 with A/B/C parts independent.
Document-Based Question: a 7-point essay built from seven documents plus thesis, contextualization, evidence, and sourcing analysis.
Placing an argument in its broader historical setting; one of the most-lost points on the DBQ and LEQ rubrics.

presentation.tone: a teacher talking to a smart 16-year-old; plain, spoken, concrete

narration.text: [beat]Here is the exam's format: short-answer, question three. No passage, no documents, just you and what you know. [pause:2] Using Unit 1: (a) Identify one similarity between Spanish and French interactions with Native peoples. (b) Identify one difference between Spanish and English colonization before 1607. (c) Explain one reason for that difference. [pause:2] If your mind went blank, that is the point. By the end, you will answer it cold.

narration.text: [beat]Unit 1 has a one-sentence thesis. Geography wrote the first draft of American history, and contact rewrote it. [beat] Every lesson supports that claim. Lesson 1: geography shaped Native societies, from Cahokia to the Iroquois. Lesson 4: alliances plus disease, not guns, decided the conquest. Lesson 7: labor reorganized, from encomienda to casta. Lesson 8: Europe asked whether conquest could be just. [beat] The rest pin to the same board: crops and diseases exchanged, the silver mountain, the revolt that drove Spain out.

narration.text: [beat]But contact did not just conquer. It mixed. Three peoples met, and something new came out. The Spanish and French intermarried with Native peoples far more than the English. Missions became contact zones where converts blended saints with spirits. That blending has a name the exam loves: syncretism. [pause:1] They misunderstood each other. Europeans owned land as property. Many Native societies held it in common. [beat] That collision is C-E-D topic 1.6, the unit thesis in miniature.

narration.text: [beat]Now the tools. The exam tests three reasoning processes, and Unit 1 fits all three. First lens: comparison. Spain: missions and Native labor. France: furs and intermarriage. England: late and fenced off. [beat] Second lens: causation. Ask why, not just what. Why did five hundred men topple an empire? Not the guns alone. Stack them: Native alliances, then smallpox. [beat] Comparison finds the pattern. Causation finds the engine.

narration.text: [beat]Third lens: continuity and change. Ask what contact altered and what survived it. Labor changed completely. The encomienda gave way to African slavery. But forced labor survived, and so did European rivalry. [beat] Then comes 1588. England's defeat of the Spanish Armada broke Spain's lock on the ocean. Before it, Spain's navy could crush any rival colony. After it, France and England could and did. [beat] One sea battle. Period 2 becomes possible. That is continuity and change in a single date. [pause:2]

narration.text: [beat]The format, checked against the current prep book. Three questions. One and two are required; you choose three or four. Question one: secondary sources to pick apart. Question two: a primary source testing comparison or causation. [beat] Question three is the Unit 1 question: no stimulus, Periods 1 through 5, straight from memory. Parts score alone, so a blank (a) never kills (b) or (c). Answer all three. [beat] On essays, two habits earn the most-lost points. Contextualization: set the broader scene before your argument, on the D-B-Q and the L-E-Q. On the D-B-Q, use at least four documents. Six earns the full evidence credit. Explain point of view or purpose; never just quote.

narration.text: [beat]Back to the question. (a) The Spanish and French intermarried and traded with Native peoples, unlike the English. (b) Spain built missions and a forced-labor empire in the 1500s. England's colonies came after 1607 and excluded Native peoples. (c) Spain's navy kept rivals out until England defeated the Armada in 1588. [beat] Three parts, three points. That is the whole game.
